newsitem.title: USA: Florida freeze to cause "some yield loss" - growers.
newsitem.headline: Florida freeze to cause "some yield loss" - growers.

text.p: Unseasonably chilly weekend temperatures will mean "some loss" of orange juice yield for Florida growers that could force wholesale prices slightly higher, the head of the Florida Citrus Mutual cooperative said Monday.

Temperatures early Sunday dipped into the mid-20s throughout much of central Florida, with a small area recording a low of 19 degrees, said Bobby McKown, executive director of the growers' cooperative.

"Our early estimate is that we will have some loss in juice yield, that we'll get less juice from each box of fruit," he said. "It wasn't a killer freeze like in the 1980s. But we'll have some twig and leaf damage, and some damage to speciality fruit that remained on the trees."

McKown said he could not yet quantify the impact on juice yield until more information was collected from growers, but said the freezing temperatures covered most of the state's citrus-growing belt. "It's a big part of the crop, and most of the area was affected," he said.

Early Sunday, temperatures dipped lower than the National Weather Service had forecast, mostly because expected cloud cover failed to move over central Florida. Temperatures remained below the freezing mark for one to eight hours, depending on the location, McKown said.

"We've got a wait-and-see attitude about the damage. Retail prices are already high and we don't see any pressure for retail prices to go up. Wholesale prices could firm up just a little bit as a result of the yield loss," he said.
Florida state agricultural officials said the weekend freeze affected citrus crops along the state's west coast and farther south than expected.

Terry McElroy, spokesman for the Florida Department of Agriculture, said many growers were taken by surprise as weather forecasts had predicted less-severe temperatures because of anticipated cloud cover over the state.

Agriculture department assessors were in the fields to determine the extent of damage to the citrus crop as well as fruit and vegetable yields. "It may be a day or so before we can quantify it," McElroy said.

Citrus can be damaged when temperatures fall below 27 degrees Fahrenheit for four hours or more. Although many growers used sprayers to coat fruit with water for insulation, the temperatures remained colder for much longer than had been expected, McKown said.
As of Jan. 12, about 67 percent of Florida's citrus crop was still on the trees, he said.

According to earlier U.S. Agriculture Department forecasts, Florida growers were expected to harvest 220 million boxes of oranges and 59 million boxes of grapefruits. Citrus is Florida's second-largest industry, with an annual impact of $8 billion, according to state officials.

In south Florida, where winter fruits and vegetables are raised, growers also reported some damage to green beans, bananas, corn and other crops. Temperatures were recorded in the low 30s a few miles south of Miami.
